Poisson Regression: A Guide in Simplified Technical English

1. About this paper

This paper teaches Poisson regression. It gives all the concepts, skills and examples from Chapter 11 (Section 11.2) of Statistical Rethinking, second edition, by Richard McElreath. It is not a summary. Each idea from the chapter is in this paper.

Who this paper is for. This paper is for students who use English as a second language. The text uses ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (STE). STE has these rules:

  • Sentences are short. Each sentence gives one idea.

  • Each word has one meaning. The paper uses the same word for the same thing each time.

  • Instructions use the imperative form, for example "Calculate the mean."

  • Technical terms are in bold when they first occur. Section 10 gives a glossary of these terms. The symbol ᴳ after a term shows a link to its glossary entry.

  • If you like STE, ask your AI chat bot to write using ASD-STE100.

The code. The code is in Python, with PyMC and ArviZ. Run the code blocks in order. Each block uses the variables from the blocks before it. MCMC and the simulations are random, so your numbers can be a little different from the numbers in this paper. Python counts from 0, so the first category of an index variableᴳ has index 0.

2. From binomial to Poisson

Main point: When the number of trials is very large and the probability of an event is very small, the binomial distribution becomes the Poisson distribution. The Poisson distribution has one parameter. This parameter is both the mean and the variance.

2.1 Counts with no known upper limit

Use a binomial GLM when the outcome is a count from zero to a known upper limit. If you can compare the data to the globe-tossing model, use a binomial GLM.

But often the upper limit is not known. Also, the counts are often far below any upper limit. For example, you go fishing and you catch 17 fish. What was the maximum number of fish that you could catch? The data do not tell you. How do we model these counts?

The binomial model also works here, with one special condition. For a binomial distribution with N trials and probability p:

  • The expected value is Np.

  • The variance is Np(1 − p).

When N is very large and p is very small, (1 − p) is almost 1. Thus, the mean and the variance are approximately the same.

2.2 Example: the monastery

You own a monastery that copies manuscripts by hand. You have 1000 monks. On a typical day, approximately 1 monk completes a manuscript. The monks work independently, and the manuscripts have different lengths. Thus, the number of manuscripts changes from day to day. Some days produce 3 or more manuscripts. Many days produce none.

This is a binomial process with N = 1000 and p = 0.001. Thus:

  • The mean is Np = 1000 × 0.001 = 1.

  • The variance is Np(1 − p) = 1000 × 0.001 × 0.999 ≈ 1.

First, run the setup block. It imports the packages and sets the colours for the figures.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pymc as pm
import arviz as az
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DARK, BLUE = "#333333", "#2a78d6"   # colours for the figures
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
                     "figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10})
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)

Then simulate the monastery for 100,000 days:

y = rng.binomial(1000, 1 / 1000, 100_000)   # 100,000 days, 1000 monks, p = 0.001
print(y.mean(), y.var())
0.99558 0.9958804636

The mean and the variance are almost the same. This special shape of the binomial is the Poisson distributionᴳ. It is useful because it lets us model binomial events when the number of trials N is not known, or is too large to count.

An example: you get a second monastery. You do not know how many monks work in it. Your advisors tell you that it makes 2 manuscripts per day on average. With only this information, you can know the distribution of the number of manuscripts for each day. It is a Poisson distribution with a mean of 2.

2.3 The Poisson model

The Poisson distribution has only one parameter, λ (lambda). Thus, the model is very simple:

yi∼Poisson(λ)y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)

The parameter λ is the expected value of the outcome y. It is also the expected variance of the counts.

We also need a link function. The usual link function for a Poisson model is the log linkᴳ (Chapter 10 in the textbook). Thus, a Poisson GLM with one predictor x is:

yi∼Poisson(λi)log⁡(λi)=α+β(xi−xˉ)\begin{aligned} y_i &\sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i) \\ \log(\lambda_i) &= \alpha + \beta (x_i - \bar{x}) \end{aligned}

The log link makes sure that λ is always positive. The expected value of a count must be positive.

But the log link also gives an exponential relationshipᴳ between the predictors and the expected value. Exponential relationships increase very quickly. Few natural processes can stay exponential for a long time. Thus, do these checks with a log link:

  1. Make sure that the relationship is sensible for all values of the predictor.

  2. Use prior predictive simulationᴳ. Priors on the log scale change in surprising ways on the outcome scale.

3. Example: Oceanic tool complexity

Main point: The data are tool counts for 10 island societies in Oceania. The research question is this: do larger and better-connected populations have more types of tools?

3.1 A natural experiment

The island societies of Oceania give a natural experimentᴳ in technological evolution. Different island populations had tool kits of different sizes. The tool kits included fish hooks, axes, boats, hand plows and many other types of tools.

Some theories predict that larger populations make and keep more complex tool kits. Island size, and thus population size, changes naturally across Oceania. Thus, we can use the islands to test this idea.

Other theories say that contactᴳ between populations has the same effect as a larger population. Thus, the contact rate between societies is also important.

3.2 Load the data

The data are counts of unique tool types in 10 historical Oceanic societies. The file Kline2.csv has the same data as the textbook, and also the latitude and longitude of each society.

DATA = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pymc-devs/pymc-resources/main/Rethinking_2/Data/"
d = pd.read_csv(DATA + "Kline2.csv")
d[["culture", "population", "contact", "total_tools", "mean_TU"]]

This is the full data set. Plot the location of each society:

lon = d["lon"] % 360                 # 0 to 360, so that the Pacific is in one piece
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.axhline(0, color="#999999", lw=1, ls="--")       # the Equator
ax.axvline(180, color="#999999", lw=1, ls=":")      # the International Date Line

Figure 1. The locations of the 10 societies in the data. The dashed line is the Equator. The dotted line is the International Date Line.

The sample size. In a count model, the number of rows is not the same as the "sample size". The relation between the parameters and the "degrees of freedom" is not simple, except in simple linear regressions. There are not many data here, because there are not many historical Oceanic societies with good data. Thus, use regularizing priors to prevent overfittingᴳ. But you can still learn from these data.

The textbook says that rules about a minimum sample size for inference are not part of Bayesian inference. If the posterior is almost the same as the prior, then the data are not sufficient. It is that simple.

3.3 The hypotheses

The outcome variable is total_tools. We will test these three ideas:

  1. The number of tools increases with the log of the population. Why log? The theory says that the order of magnitude of the population is important, not its absolute size. Thus, we look for a positive association between total_tools and log population. Section 7 shows why a linear effect of population size cannot be correct.

  2. The number of tools increases with the contact rate among islands. Islands with better networks can get or keep more tool types.

  3. The effect of population on tools is larger or smaller when contact is high. This is an interactionᴳ: the association between total_tools and log population depends on contact. We look for a positive interaction between log population and contact rate.

3.4 Make the variables

Make a standardizedᴳ log population P. Make an index variable cid for contact:

d["P"] = (np.log(d["population"]) - np.log(d["population"]).mean()) / np.log(d["population"]).std()
d["cid"] = (d["contact"] == "high").astype(int)     # 0 = low contact, 1 = high contact

4. Find the priors with prior predictive simulation

Main point: With a log link, a flat prior on the linear model makes absurd predictions on the count scale. Use α ~ Normal(3, 0.5) and β ~ Normal(0, 0.2).

4.1 The model

The model for the research hypothesis has an interaction between population and contact rate:

Ti∼Poisson(λi)log⁡λi=αCID[i]+βCID[i]log⁡Piαj∼to be determinedβj∼to be determined\begin{aligned} T_i &\sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i) \\ \log \lambda_i &= \alpha_{\text{CID}[i]} + \beta_{\text{CID}[i]} \log P_i \\ \alpha_j &\sim \text{to be determined} \\ \beta_j &\sim \text{to be determined} \end{aligned}

In this model, T is total_tools, P is population, and CID is the contact index. Each contact level has its own intercept and its own slope. This is how the model includes the interaction.

We must find sensible priors. The link function changes the scale between the linear model and the outcome. Thus, a prior that is flat on the linear-model scale is not flat on the outcome scale.

4.2 The prior for the intercept

Start with a model that has only an intercept and a flat prior:

Ti∼Poisson(λi)log⁡λi=αα∼Normal(0,10)\begin{aligned} T_i &\sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i) \\ \log \lambda_i &= \alpha \\ \alpha &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 10) \end{aligned}

What does this prior mean on the outcome scale, λ? If α has a normal distribution, then λ = exp(α) has a log-normal distributionᴳ. Plot the log-normal distribution for this prior and for a better prior, Normal(3, 0.5):

x = np.linspace(0, 100, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.4))
ax.plot(x, stats.lognorm.pdf(x, s=10, scale=np.exp(0)), color=DARK, lw=2)
ax.plot(x, stats.lognorm.pdf(x, s=0.5, scale=np.exp(3)), color=BLUE, lw=2)
ax.text(8, 0.06, "a ~ Normal(0, 10)", color=DARK)
ax.text(30, 0.035, "a ~ Normal(3, 0.5)", color=BLUE)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.08)
ax.set_xlabel("mean number of tools")
ax.set_ylabel("density")
plt.show()

Figure 2. Prior predictive distribution of the mean λ for a Poisson model with only an intercept. Dark: the flat prior Normal(0, 10) gives absurd expectations. Blue: Normal(3, 0.5) moves the prior mass above zero.

The horizontal axis goes from 0 to 100. We know that all historical tool kits were in this range.

The Normal(0, 10) prior (dark) has a very large peak near zero. This means zero tools on average. It also has a very long tail. How long? The mean of a log-normal distribution is exp(μ + σ²/2). Here, this is exp(50). This number is impossibly large. Do a simulation to see this:

a = rng.normal(0, 10, 10_000)
lam = np.exp(a)
print(lam.mean())                     # a very, very large number
print(np.exp(0 + 10**2 / 2))          # the mean of the log-normal: exp(50)
print(np.exp(3 + 0.5**2 / 2))         # the mean for Normal(3, 0.5): about 20
350610675600.27246
5.184705528587072e+21
22.75989509352673

That is enough tools to cover a full island. We can do better.

Try different means and standard deviations in the code. The important fact is this: a log link puts half of the real numbers (all the negative numbers) between 0 and 1 on the outcome scale. Thus, if most of the prior is below zero, then most of the outcome is between 0 and 1. For Poisson models, flat priors do not make sense.

The Normal(3, 0.5) prior (blue) is a weakly informative prior. Its mean on the outcome scale is exp(3 + 0.5²/2) ≈ 20 (the simulation above gives approximately 23). We did not look at the mean of total_tools to make this prior. This is a prior, so it must not use the sample. We only want the prior predictive distribution to be in the range of plausible outcomes.

4.3 The prior for the slope

Now find a prior for β, the coefficient of log population. First, try a flat prior, β ~ Normal(0, 10). Simulate 100 prior trends of total tools against standardized log population. Then do the same for β ~ Normal(0, 0.2):

N = 100
x_seq = np.linspace(-2, 2, 100)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6))
for ax, sd_b in zip(axes, [10, 0.2]):
    a = rng.normal(3, 0.5, N)
    b = rng.normal(0, sd_b, N)
    for i in range(N):
        ax.plot(x_seq, np.exp(a[i] + b[i] * x_seq), color=DARK, lw=0.6, alpha=0.6)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
    ax.set_xlabel("log population (std)")
    ax.set_ylabel("total tools")
    ax.set_title(f"b ~ Normal(0, {sd_b})")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Figure 3. Prior predictive trends for the slope. Left: the flat prior Normal(0, 10) gives explosive trends. Right: the regularizing prior Normal(0, 0.2) keeps most trends in the range of possible outcomes.

Look at the left plot. All trends turn around zero. This is sensible, because zero is the average log population. The values on the horizontal axis are z-scores, because the variable is standardized.

This prior says that most relationships between log population and total tools have one of two forms:

  • Explosive growth just above the mean log population.

  • A catastrophic decrease just below the mean log population.

This prior is very bad. When you fit the models, you will see that even 10 observations can overcome it. But we practise for the cases where the prior is important. In some applications, it is important.

The textbook does not force β to be positive. The data can show this. In place of that, the prior Normal(0, 0.2) reduces the probability of impossibly explosive relationships. Look at the right plot. Strong relationships are still possible. But most of the prior gives relatively flat relationships between total tools and log population.

4.4 The priors on the natural scales

The standardized log population is good for fitting the model. But it is bad for thinking. Population has a natural zero, and we want to see it. Standardization removes it. Thus, plot 100 prior trends against log population that is not standardized (left), and against population (right):

x_seq = np.linspace(np.log(100), np.log(200_000), 100)
a = rng.normal(3, 0.5, N)
b = rng.normal(0, 0.2, N)
lam = np.exp(a[:, None] + b[:, None] * x_seq[None, :])   # N trends x 100 points

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6))
for i in range(N):
    axes[0].plot(x_seq, lam[i], color=DARK, lw=0.6, alpha=0.6)
    axes[1].plot(np.exp(x_seq), lam[i], color=DARK, lw=0.6, alpha=0.6)
axes[0].set_xlabel("log population")
axes[1].set_xlabel("population")
axes[1].set_xticks([0, 100_000, 200_000], ["0", "100,000", "200,000"])
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_ylim(0, 500)
    ax.set_ylabel("total tools")
    ax.set_title("a ~ Normal(3, 0.5), b ~ Normal(0, 0.2)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Figure 4. The same priors on natural scales. Left: the horizontal axis is log population that is not standardized. Right: the horizontal axis is population.

Look at the left plot. We probably will not see more than 100 tools in these data. Most trends stay in that range, but some explosive trends remain.

Now look at the right plot. On the population scale, the curves bend in the other direction. This is because the model uses the log of population. A Poisson model with a log link makes log-linearᴳ relationships with its predictors. When the predictor is itself a log, the model has diminishing returnsᴳ on the raw variable. Each additional person adds a smaller increase in the expected number of tools. Thus, the curves bend down and become level.

Compare the two plots. The curves on the left would be straight lines if you used a log scale for the vertical axis. Many predictor variables are better as logarithms for this reason. Prior predictive simulation is a good way to think about these problems.

5. Fit the models and compare them

Main point: The model with fewer parameters can have a larger effective number of parametersᴳ. Overfitting risk depends on the structure of the model and on the sample, not only on the number of parameters.

5.1 Fit two models

Fit the interaction model from Section 4.1 (m11.10). Also fit a very simple model with only an intercept (m11.9). The intercept-only model is here to show an interesting fact about model complexity.

T = d["total_tools"].values
P = d["P"].values
cid = d["cid"].values

# intercept only
with pm.Model() as m11_9:
    a = pm.Normal("a", 3, 0.5)
    pm.Poisson("T", mu=pm.math.exp(a), observed=T)
    idata_11_9 = pm.sample(1000, chains=4, random_seed=1,
                           idata_kwargs={"log_likelihood": True})

# interaction model
with pm.Model(coords={"contact": ["low", "high"]}) as m11_10:
    a = pm.Normal("a", 3, 0.5, dims="contact")
    b = pm.Normal("b", 0, 0.2, dims="contact")
    lam = pm.math.exp(a[cid] + b[cid] * P)
    pm.Poisson("T", mu=lam, observed=T)
    idata_11_10 = pm.sample(1000, chains=4, random_seed=1,
                            idata_kwargs={"log_likelihood": True})

az.summary(idata_11_10, var_names=["a", "b"], ci_prob=0.89).round(2)
Parametermeansd5.5%94.5%
a[low]3.320.093.203.50
a[high]3.610.073.503.70
b[low]0.380.050.290.46
b[high]0.190.16-0.060.45

5.2 Compare the models with PSIS

cmp = az.compare({"m11.9": idata_11_9, "m11.10": idata_11_10}, round_to=None)
cmp["PSIS"] = -2 * cmp["elpd"]          # deviance scale, as in the textbook
cmp[["PSIS", "p", "weight"]].round(1)
ModelPSISEffective parameters (p)weight
m11.10 (interaction)approximately 846.81.0
m11.9 (intercept only)approximately 1428.90.0

As in the binomial paper, ArviZ gives elpd. The code converts it to the deviance scale of the textbook: PSIS = −2 × elpd. A smaller PSIS is better. The textbook gets PSIS values of 85.5 and 141.1, with 7.1 and 8.0 effective parameters.

This result shows two important facts.

Fact 1: the Pareto k warning. ArviZ reports high Pareto kᴳ values for both models. This shows that some points have a large influence. This is not a surprise, because the sample is small. But we must think about these points when we look at the posterior predictions (Section 6).

Fact 2: the effective number of parameters. The intercept-only model m11.9 has a worse PSIS than the interaction model m11.10. This is not a surprise. But look at the effective number of parameters, p. It is larger for m11.9, the model with fewer parameters. Model m11.9 has only one parameter. Model m11.10 has four parameters. This is not a strange property of PSIS. WAIC gives the same result.

5.3 Why the simpler model has more effective parameters

The number of parameters and the model complexity (the tendency of a model to overfit) have a clear relationship only in one case: a simple linear regression with flat priors.

In other models, the relationship is not simple. For example, when a distribution has a boundary, parameter values near the boundary cause less overfitting than values far from the boundary. The same is true for the data. A count near zero is difficult to overfit. Thus, the risk of overfitting depends on two things:

  • The structural details of the model.

  • The composition of the sample.

In this sample, the highly influential points are a large source of overfitting risk. Section 6 looks at these points.

6. Posterior predictions

Main point: Hawaii has a very large influence on the posterior. Also, the conventional model lets the trend for high contact go below the trend for low contact. This does not make sense.

6.1 Find the influential points

Get the Pareto k value of each society from PSIS:

loo_10 = az.loo(idata_11_10, pointwise=True)
k = np.asarray(loo_10.pareto_k)
pd.Series(k, index=d["culture"]).round(2).sort_values(ascending=False)
culturePareto k
Tonga0.74
Hawaii0.64
Trobriand0.52
Tikopia0.46
Malekula0.45
Yap0.42
Santa Cruz0.29
Lau Fiji0.25
Manus0.17
Chuuk0.15

The textbook gets these values: Hawaii 1.01, Tonga 0.69, Yap 0.6 and Trobriand 0.56. Your values can be different, because Pareto k values from only 10 points are not stable. The values change with the MCMC samples. But Hawaii and Tonga are always among the most influential points.

6.2 Plot the predictions

Plot the data and the posterior predictions of the expected number of tools for each population size and contact rate. The size of each point shows its Pareto k value. Plot the predictions on two scales: standardized log population (left) and population (right). To get the natural scale, reverse the standardization. For the right plot, start the sequence at −5. Then the curves start near zero population.

post = idata_11_10.posterior.to_dataset().stack(s=("chain", "draw"))
a_s, b_s = post["a"].values, post["b"].values          # 2 x samples each
log_pop = np.log(d["population"])
size = 20 + 200 * (k - k.min()) / (k.max() - k.min())    # bigger point = larger k

# left: standardized log population; right: population (natural scale)
P_left = np.linspace(-1.4, 3, 100)
P_right = np.linspace(-5, 3, 100)                         # starts near zero population
pop_right = np.exp(P_right * log_pop.std() + log_pop.mean())  # reverse the standardization

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
panels = [(axes[0], P_left, P_left, d["P"]),
          (axes[1], P_right, pop_right, d["population"])]
for ax, P_seq, xs, xdata in panels:
    for c, ls in [(1, "-"), (0, "--")]:                  # high contact solid, low dashed
        lam = np.exp(a_s[c][:, None] + b_s[c][:, None] * P_seq[None, :])
        lo, hi = np.percentile(lam, [5.5, 94.5], axis=0)
        ax.fill_between(xs, lo, hi, color="#000000", alpha=0.12, lw=0)
        ax.plot(xs, lam.mean(axis=0), color=DARK, ls=ls, lw=1.8)
    high = d["cid"] == 1
    ax.scatter(xdata[high], d["total_tools"][high], s=size[high], color=BLUE, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(xdata[~high], d["total_tools"][~high], s=size[~high], facecolors="white",
               edgecolors=BLUE, lw=1.5, zorder=3)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 75)
    ax.set_ylabel("total tools")
for i in np.argsort(k)[-4:]:                             # label the 4 largest k values
    axes[0].text(d["P"][i] + 0.08, d["total_tools"][i] + 2,
                 f"{d['culture'][i]} ({k[i]:.2f})", fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_xlim(-1.5, 2.6)
axes[1].set_xlim(-5000, 290_000)
axes[0].set_xlabel("log population (std)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("population")
axes[1].set_xticks([0, 100_000, 200_000], ["0", "100,000", "200,000"])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Figure 5. Posterior predictions for the Oceanic tools model m11.10. Filled points: societies with high contact. Open points: societies with low contact. Larger points have larger Pareto k values. Solid curve: posterior mean for high contact. Dashed curve: posterior mean for low contact. Shaded regions: 89% intervals. Left: standardized log population. Right: the same predictions on the population scale.

6.3 Hawaii is very influential

Hawaii has the largest population and the most tools. You can see this most clearly on the population scale (right). This does not mean that Hawaii is an "outlier" that we must remove from the data. But it does mean that Hawaii has a strong effect on the posterior distribution. A practice problem in the textbook asks you to remove Hawaii and see what changes.

6.4 A problem with the trends

Look at the posterior predictions again. When population is small, the trend for high contact (solid) is above the trend for low contact (dashed). But at large population sizes, the model lets the high-contact trend be lower than the low-contact trend.

The model does not really know where the high-contact trend goes at large population sizes. There are no societies in the data with a large population and high contact. There is only Hawaii, which has low contact. But the pattern is still silly. A hypothetical Hawaii with the same population but high contact should have at least as many tools as the real Hawaii. It must not have fewer.

The model can make this silly pattern because the intercept is free. Thus, there is no guarantee that the trend for λ goes through the origin, where both the total tools and the population are zero. When there are zero people, there are also zero tools. When population increases, tools increase. If we think about the problem, we get the intercept with no cost. Section 7 shows a model that uses this idea.

7. A scientific model of tool innovation and loss

Main point: A model that comes from scientific knowledge about the process makes the trends go through the origin. Its parameters also have a meaning outside a linear model.

7.1 From a verbal model to a mathematical model

In place of the conventional GLM, we can use the predictions of a real model of the relationship between population size and tools. A "real model" is a model that comes from scientific knowledge and from hypothetical causal effects. The disadvantage is that it feels less like statistics, because knowledge of the subject is necessary. The advantage is that it feels more like science.

We want a dynamic modelᴳ of the cultural evolution of tools. Tools do not appear all at the same time. They develop over time:

  • Innovationᴳ adds tools.

  • Lossᴳ removes tools.

These two processes come to a balance. The balance gives tool kits of different sizes.

The simplest model makes these assumptions:

  • Innovation is proportional to population size, with diminishing returns. The diminishing returns are an elasticityᴳ.

  • Tool loss is proportional to the number of tools, with no diminishing returns.

This is the type of model in the neutral evolution debate (Chapter 1 in the textbook). The full theoretical model is more complex than the model here.

The change in the expected number of tools in one time step is:

ΔT=αPβ−γT\Delta T = \alpha P^{\beta} - \gamma T

In this equation, P is the population size, T is the number of tools, and α, β and γ are parameters to estimate. To find the equilibriumᴳ number of tools, set ΔT = 0 and solve for T:

T^=αPβγ\hat{T} = \frac{\alpha P^{\beta}}{\gamma}

Use this in a Poisson model. The noise around the outcome is still Poisson, because the Poisson distribution is still the maximum entropyᴳ distribution here: a count with no clear upper limit. But there is no linear model:

Ti∼Poisson(λi)λi=αPiβ/γ\begin{aligned} T_i &\sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i) \\ \lambda_i &= \alpha P_i^{\beta} / \gamma \end{aligned}

There is no link function. We must only make sure that λ is positive. To do this, make sure that the parameters are positive:

  • Use exp(a) in place of α, with a ~ Normal(1, 1). Then α has a log-normal prior and is always positive.

  • Use exponential priors for β and γ. Exponential priors give only positive values.

We also let the parameters change with the contact rate. Contact is supposed to change the effect of population size, so we let α and β change with contact. Contact can also have an effect on γ, because trade networks can prevent the loss of tools. The textbook leaves this as an exercise.

7.2 Fit the model

The textbook chose the priors without showing the steps. Use prior predictive simulation to test them. Now the parameters have a meaning, so it is easier to design the priors. The important lesson is how the model includes the predictor variables.

Pop = d["population"].values
with pm.Model(coords={"contact": ["low", "high"]}) as m11_11:
    a = pm.Normal("a", 1, 1, dims="contact")
    b = pm.Exponential("b", 1, dims="contact")
    g = pm.Exponential("g", 1)
    lam = pm.math.exp(a[cid]) * Pop ** b[cid] / g        # no link function
    pm.Poisson("T", mu=lam, observed=T)
    idata_11_11 = pm.sample(1000, chains=4, random_seed=1, target_accept=0.99,
                            idata_kwargs={"log_likelihood": True})

az.summary(idata_11_11, var_names=["a", "b", "g"], ci_prob=0.89).round(2)
Parametermeansd5.5%94.5%
a[low]0.900.70-0.232.00
a[high]0.930.86-0.432.20
b[low]0.260.030.210.32
b[high]0.290.100.120.46
g1.150.780.302.60

The option target_accept=0.99 makes the sampler take smaller steps. With the default value, this model gives some divergent transitions.

The code for the posterior predictions is almost the same as in Section 6.2. Use the new formula for λ:

post = idata_11_11.posterior.to_dataset().stack(s=("chain", "draw"))
a_s, b_s, g_s = post["a"].values, post["b"].values, post["g"].values
pop_seq = np.linspace(0, 280_000, 200)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
for c, ls, label in [(1, "-", "high contact"), (0, "--", "low contact")]:
    lam = np.exp(a_s[c])[:, None] * pop_seq[None, :] ** b_s[c][:, None] / g_s[:, None]
    lo, hi = np.percentile(lam, [5.5, 94.5], axis=0)
    ax.fill_between(pop_seq, lo, hi, color="#000000", alpha=0.12, lw=0)
    ax.plot(pop_seq, lam.mean(axis=0), color=DARK, ls=ls, lw=1.8, label=label)
high = d["cid"] == 1
ax.scatter(d["population"][high], d["total_tools"][high], s=size[high], color=BLUE, zorder=3)
ax.scatter(d["population"][~high], d["total_tools"][~high], s=size[~high],
           facecolors="white", edgecolors=BLUE, lw=1.5, zorder=3)
ax.set_ylim(0, 75)
ax.set_xticks([0, 100_000, 200_000], ["0", "100,000", "200,000"])
ax.set_xlabel("population")
ax.set_ylabel("total tools")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

Figure 6. Posterior predictions for the scientific model m11.11 of the Oceanic tool counts. Compare with the right plot of Figure 5. This model forces the trends to go through the origin.

7.3 What the scientific model shows

We call the first model (m11.10) the geocentric modelᴳ, and m11.11 the scientific modelᴳ. Compare Figure 6 with the right plot of Figure 5:

  • The trend for high contact is always above the trend for low contact.

  • Both trends go through the origin, as they must.

The scientific model is not perfect. But it is a better base to learn from. The parameters have clearer meanings now. They are not only gears at the bottom of a tide-prediction machine.

How does the scientific model compare with the geocentric model? Compare them with PSIS:

az.compare({"m11.10": idata_11_10, "m11.11": idata_11_11}, round_to=None)[["elpd", "p"]]
ModelPSIS (−2 × elpd)Effective parameters (p)
m11.11 (scientific)approximately 825.7
m11.10 (geocentric)approximately 846.8

The expected accuracy out of sample is a few points better for the scientific model. WAIC gives the same result. Hawaii and Tonga still have a strong effect on the model. A later chapter in the textbook uses a different method for the contact rate: it uses how near the societies are to each other.

8. Negative-binomial (gamma-Poisson) models

Main point: Poisson models often have more variation than the model expects. The gamma-Poisson distribution is a common way to include this variation.

Usually, a Poisson model has much variation that it does not explain. This variation probably comes from unobserved effects that change from case to case. These effects make the true λ values different between cases.

If you ignore this variation, which is called rate heterogeneityᴳ, you can get confounds. The same is true for binomial models.

A very common extension of Poisson GLMs is to replace the Poisson distribution with the negative-binomial distributionᴳ. The negative-binomial distribution is really a Poisson distribution in disguise. It is a mixtureᴳ of different Poisson distributions. For this reason, people also call it the gamma-Poisson distributionᴳ. The next chapter in the textbook explains mixtures.

9. Example: exposure and the offset

Main point: When counts come from different lengths of time or space, add the log of the exposure to the linear model. This term is the offset. It has no parameter.

9.1 λ is a rate

The parameter λ is the expected value of a Poisson model. But we can also think of λ as a rateᴳ. Both meanings are correct. The rate meaning lets us make Poisson models where the exposureᴳ changes from case to case.

An example: a monastery near you counts its completed manuscripts each week. Your monastery counts them each day. You get both sets of records. How can you analyse them in the same model? The counts come from different lengths of time, so they have different exposures.

Here is the method. Implicitly, λ is equal to an expected number of events μ in a length of time or distance τ. Thus, λ = μ/τ, and the link becomes:

yi∼Poisson(λi)log⁡λi=log⁡μiτi=α+βxi\begin{aligned} y_i &\sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i) \\ \log \lambda_i &= \log \frac{\mu_i}{\tau_i} = \alpha + \beta x_i \end{aligned}

The logarithm of a ratio is the same as a difference of logarithms. Thus:

log⁡λi=log⁡μi−log⁡τi=α+βxi\log \lambda_i = \log \mu_i - \log \tau_i = \alpha + \beta x_i

The τ values are the exposures. If different observations i have different exposures, then the expected value on row i is:

log⁡μi=log⁡τi+α+βxi\log \mu_i = \log \tau_i + \alpha + \beta x_i

When τ = 1, log τ = 0, and we are back at the start. But when the exposure changes between cases, τ scales the expected number of events correctly for each case. Thus, you can model cases with different exposures with a model like this:

yi∼Poisson(μi)log⁡μi=log⁡τi+α+βxi\begin{aligned} y_i &\sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_i) \\ \log \mu_i &= \log \tau_i + \alpha + \beta x_i \end{aligned}

In this model, τ is a column in the data. It is like a predictor, the log of the exposure, but with no parameter. We can also put a parameter in front of log τ. This is one method to model the hypothesis that the rate changes with time.

9.2 Simulate two monasteries

When the length of observation, the area of sampling or the intensity of sampling changes, the counts also change. A Poisson distribution assumes that the rate of events is constant in time (or in space). Thus, it is easy to include this. Add the logarithm of the exposure to the linear model. This term is the offsetᴳ.

Simulate the data, to get more practice with dummy data and to make sure that the offset method gives the correct answer.

You own a monastery. Its records give the total number of completed manuscripts for each day. The true rate is λ = 1.5 manuscripts per day. Simulate the daily counts for one month (30 days).

You also think about buying a second monastery. You want to know how productive it is. But its owners do not keep daily records. They keep weekly totals. The true daily rate at the new monastery is λ = 0.5 manuscripts per day. To simulate weekly data, multiply this rate by 7, the exposure:

num_days = 30
y = rng.poisson(1.5, num_days)          # old monastery: 1.5 manuscripts per day

num_weeks = 4
y_new = rng.poisson(0.5 * 7, num_weeks) # new monastery: 0.5 per day, counted weekly

Now y has 30 days of counts, and y_new has 4 weeks of counts. Make one data frame for both. It shows the exposure of each case:

dm = pd.DataFrame({
    "y": np.concatenate([y, y_new]),
    "days": np.concatenate([np.ones(num_days), np.full(num_weeks, 7)]),  # exposure
    "monastery": np.concatenate([np.zeros(num_days), np.ones(num_weeks)]).astype(int),
})
dm.tail()

The data frame has three columns: the observed counts y, the number of days for each count (days), and an indicator for the new monastery (monastery).

9.3 Fit the model

Calculate the log of each exposure. Then put this variable in the linear model:

dm["log_days"] = np.log(dm["days"])
with pm.Model() as m11_12:
    a = pm.Normal("a", 0, 1)
    b = pm.Normal("b", 0, 1)
    log_lam = dm["log_days"].values + a + b * dm["monastery"].values   # offset + linear model
    pm.Poisson("y", mu=pm.math.exp(log_lam), observed=dm["y"].values)
    idata_11_12 = pm.sample(1000, chains=4, random_seed=1)

To get the posterior distribution of λ for each monastery, use the posterior samples in the linear model. Do not use the offset now. The parameters are already on the daily scale for both monasteries.

post = idata_11_12.posterior
rates = {
    "lambda_old": np.exp(post["a"]),                 # per day, old monastery
    "lambda_new": np.exp(post["a"] + post["b"]),     # per day, new monastery
}
pd.DataFrame({name: [float(v.mean()), *np.percentile(v, [5.5, 94.5])]
              for name, v in rates.items()},
             index=["mean", "5.5%", "94.5%"]).T.round(2)
mean5.5%94.5%
lambda_old1.190.901.51
lambda_new0.430.250.64

The true rates were 1.5 and 0.5. The estimates are not exactly the same, because 30 days and 4 weeks are a small sample. With a different random seed, you get different counts and different estimates.

In the textbook, the estimates are 1.34 and 0.52 manuscripts per day. Thus, the new monastery makes approximately half as many manuscripts per day as the old monastery. Here, it makes fewer than half. In both cases, the conclusion is the same: do not pay much for the new monastery.

10. Glossary

The terms are in alphabetical order. The links in the text go to these entries.

Contact

The rate of interaction between island societies, for example by trade. In the data, contact is "low" or "high".

Diminishing returns

Each additional unit of a predictor adds a smaller increase to the outcome than the unit before it.

Dynamic model

A model of how a quantity changes over time.

Effective number of parameters

A measure of the tendency of a model to overfit. PSIS and WAIC calculate it. It is not always the same as the number of parameters.

Elasticity

The proportional change in an outcome for a proportional change in a predictor. In the tool model, the parameter β is an elasticity.

Equilibrium

The value of a quantity where the changes balance, so that the quantity does not change.

Exponential relationship

A relationship where the outcome is multiplied by the same factor for each unit of the predictor. The log link gives an exponential relationship.

Exposure

The length of time, the distance or the area over which a count is made.

Gamma-Poisson distribution

Another name for the negative-binomial distribution. It is a mixture of Poisson distributions.

Geocentric model

In this paper: a conventional GLM that predicts well enough but does not come from a model of the process.

Index variable

A variable that gives each category a number (0, 1, 2, ...). Each category gets its own parameter.

Innovation

In the tool model: the process that adds new tools to a tool kit.

Interaction

The effect of one variable depends on the value of another variable.

Log link

The link function log(λ). It makes sure that λ is always positive. It is the usual link for Poisson models.

Log-linear relationship

A relationship that is linear on the log scale of the outcome.

Log-normal distribution

The distribution of exp(x) when x has a normal distribution.

Loss

In the tool model: the process that removes tools from a tool kit.

Maximum entropy

The principle that selects the most conservative distribution that agrees with what we know.

Mixture

A distribution that is a combination of several different distributions.

Natural experiment

A situation where nature, not the researcher, changes the value of a variable between cases.

Negative-binomial distribution

A distribution for counts with more variation than a Poisson distribution. It is a mixture of Poisson distributions.

Offset

The log of the exposure, added to the linear model of a Poisson GLM with no parameter.

Overfitting

A model learns too much from the sample. Then it predicts new data badly.

Pareto k

A diagnostic value from PSIS. A high value shows an observation with a large influence on the posterior.

Poisson distribution

The binomial distribution when N is very large and p is very small. It has one parameter, λ, which is both its mean and its variance.

Prior predictive simulation

A simulation from the priors, to see what the model predicts before it sees the data.

Rate

The expected number of events in one unit of time or distance.

Rate heterogeneity

Variation in the true rate λ from case to case that the model does not include.

Scientific model

In this paper: a model that comes from scientific knowledge about the process, for example tool innovation and loss.

Standardize

Subtract the mean of a variable and divide by its standard deviation. The result has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
